113.title: Kirtan at home
113.hook: many families sing a shabad in the evening or before sleep
113.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset and Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and families often sing or play a shabad at home in the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sangat singing back, the room answering the ragis. Your line was voices together.

Every home has its evening sounds. The TV murmuring in another room. A dishwasher. Someone scrolling, someone arguing about homework, a phone buzzing on the counter long after anyone should answer it. In many Punjabi homes, the evening has another sound. A grandmother on the edge of her bed, singing a shabad softly as the lights go off. A father with a small harmonium on the living room rug, a child next to him, both a little out of tune. Or a phone on the nightstand playing a hymn quietly while someone falls asleep. The gurdwara has its own evening programs. The home has every night.
screen: `THE TV IN THE NEXT ROOM.` → `A SHABAD AS THE LIGHTS GO OFF.` → `THE HOME IS EVERY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: For nine days you've been learning kirtan. Today it comes home. Sikh daily life has an evening shape. The Sikh code of conduct sets Rehras Sahib, the evening prayer, for sunset. And last thing at night, before sleep, comes Kirtan Sohila, a short set of five shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib. Its very name has kirtan in it: sohila is a song of praise, a song of joy. It's the same prayer sung when the Granth is put to rest in the gurdwara at night, and at the end of a Sikh funeral. So the day, the scripture and a life all close with it. Remember the line from day ninety-six, that in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One? It comes from Kirtan Sohila. Some Sikh children grow up falling asleep to it. Not every family recites the whole thing aloud together every night. They might sing one shabad after dinner, or play a recording as the house goes quiet, or a parent might sing one line at a bedside. It doesn't need to be polished; it's not a concert. The Gurus lived as householders, and their hymns were sung in kitchens and courtyards long before any grand building. And consider what it does to a home. The last sound of the day isn't the news, or a notification, or an argument. It's a hymn, and the rooms fill up with it. Over years, some children remember it the way others remember a lullaby. This closes the kirtan days. Tomorrow, langar.
screen: `NINE DAYS, NOW COMING HOME.` · `REHRAS AT SUNSET.` · `KIRTAN SOHILA BEFORE SLEEP.` · `THE LAST SOUND OF THE DAY.` · then, large: `THE HOME FILLS UP.`

segments.voice: Picture your room at bedtime, the light low, the phone face down on the nightstand, and sing your one line from two days ago very softly, the way you'd sing to a child who's nearly asleep, or sing Waheguru a few times. Let the sound fill the space around you, then fade, and stay in the quiet.
Kirtan Sohila. The short set of five shabads sung before sleep, and, with Rehras at sunset, part of how the Word lives in ordinary houses.
Your line: the home fills up. A hymn at bedtime doesn't need a concert hall. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: Why the floor
114.hook: in langar people sit in rows on the floor, everyone level, whoever they are
114.howItsDone: In langar halls people traditionally sit on the floor in long rows, the pangat, and are served the same food by volunteers; some gurdwaras also provide chairs for elders and those who cannot sit on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirtan Sohila, the last sound before sleep. Your line was the home fills up.

In a restaurant, look at the chairs. The booth by the window. The stool at the bar. The high chair for the baby. The corner table where the owner seats his friends. Chairs sort us: by money, by age, by who we know. Now take the chairs away. All of them. Put long strips of cloth on the floor, in straight lines, and ask everyone who walks in to sit on them, cross-legged, shoulder to shoulder. The man who owns six restaurants sits there. So does the man who washes their dishes. You met this picture on day two. Now, six days of langar, starting with the row itself.
screen: `CHAIRS SORT US.` → `TAKE THEM ALL AWAY.` → `LONG STRIPS OF CLOTH ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Pangat. A row, a line of people sitting together to eat. In langar, it's the long line on the floor, side by side, everyone served the same food. You met a saying on day fifty-one: first the pangat, then the sangat. Tradition says Guru Amar Das asked everyone who came to see him to sit and eat in the row first, whoever they were. The story goes that even the emperor Akbar sat on the floor and ate before he met the Guru. Why the floor? Because it's the one place where no one can be higher. A chair can be taller, a table can be at the front, a seat can be closer to the kitchen. But the floor is the floor. It's humble in a physical way too: it's hard to feel grand with your knees folded under you and a plate in your hands. And the row has no head; no end of the line counts more than the other. The Guru Granth Sahib has a line that Sikhs connect with this. Guru Arjan says, in paraphrase, that all are sharers in God's grace, and no one is seen to be outside it. The pangat puts that on the ground where you can see it. In recent decades, some gurdwaras abroad argued bitterly over tables and chairs in the langar hall, and the Akal Takht ruled for the floor. Today some gurdwaras keep the floor and also set chairs aside for elders and anyone who can't sit down low. The row still holds.

segments.voice: If you can, sit on the floor, cross-legged or however is comfortable; if you can't, sink a little lower in your seat and feel the ground under you. Picture a long row stretching out on both sides, filled with real people: someone you admire, someone you find difficult, someone you've never met. Everybody at the same height, waiting for the same food.

115.title: The kitchen door stays open
115.hook: langar is free to anyone of any background, in many gurdwaras all day
115.howItsDone: Langar is served free in every gurdwara to anyone who comes, and in many it runs all day; visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes, and Sikh volunteers also run langar kitchens at disasters and for travelers in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pangat, the row on the floor where no one sits higher. Your line was same row.

It's two in the afternoon on a Tuesday. You're a college student far from home, down to your last few dollars. Or a truck driver who's been on the road since four. Or someone who just lost a job and hasn't told anyone yet. You walk past a gurdwara, and someone at the door waves you in. You don't know a word of Punjabi. You don't know what a Sikh believes. You're not sure you're allowed. You cover your head with a borrowed scarf, take off your shoes, sit down in the row, and a stranger puts hot food in your hands. Nobody asks your name. Nobody asks why you're hungry.
screen: `TWO IN THE AFTERNOON, TUESDAY.` → `WAVED IN AT THE DOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Langar is free, and it's for anyone: any faith or none, any background, any reason for being hungry, or no reason at all. That's not a side rule. It's the whole point. In many gurdwaras the kitchen runs all day, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar it feeds tens of thousands of people every single day, around the clock. Remember its four doors from day sixty, facing every direction so anyone from anywhere could walk in? The kitchen has the same shape. No ticket, no sermon to sit through first, no form to fill in. You do cover your head and take off your shoes, as everyone does. That's respect, not a test. Guru Nanak gives a picture in the Japji that fits the langar hall. In paraphrase: let wisdom be your food, and compassion the one who hands it out. And Sikhs have taken the open door far beyond the gurdwara. After floods and earthquakes, at borders, on highways where travelers are stranded, Sikh volunteers set up kitchens and start serving, often before anyone official arrives. The food is simple. The rule is the same. The open door asks something of the people inside, too: not just to cook, but to keep noticing who isn't in the room yet. The student. The driver. The person who's embarrassed to come. The door isn't really open if nobody ever walks out of it to wave someone in.
screen: `FREE, FOR ANYONE.` · `FOUR DOORS, ONE KITCHEN.` · `COMPASSION HANDS OUT THE FOOD.` · `NOTICE WHO ISN'T IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Picture the places you move through in a normal week: your street, your work or school, the store, the bus. In your mind, look for the people who might be hungry, or lonely at mealtimes, the new coworker who eats alone, the neighbor who lives by himself, the person you pass on the corner every day, and let each face come and stay a moment. Don't plan anything big yet; just notice them.
Langar. The Guru's kitchen, free to anyone, of any faith or none, no questions asked, in many places all day.
Your line: the door stays open. Any faith or none, nobody asks why. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: Rolling rotis
116.hook: kneading and rolling bread in the langar is seva with dough
116.howItsDone: Volunteers in gurdwara kitchens knead, roll and cook rotis for langar, often sitting together on the floor; newcomers are welcome to learn, and in the largest kitchens machines help alongside hand-rolling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar's open door: any faith or none, no questions asked. Your line was the door stays open.

Sunday morning in the back of a busy gurdwara kitchen: the smell of flour and hot iron. Around a low table, a circle of women and men sit on the floor with rolling pins. One pinches off balls of dough. The next flattens them. The next rolls them into circles, with a little flick after every push. Nearby, someone flips them on a huge, flat iron griddle, then onto the open flame for a second, where they puff up like small balloons. Flour on everyone's arms. Gossip, laughter, a shabad playing on someone's phone. And a stack of rotis growing taller by the minute.
screen: `FLOUR AND HOT IRON.` → `PINCH, FLATTEN, ROLL, FLIP.` → `A STACK GROWING TALLER.`

segments.voice: Roti is the simple flatbread at the center of a Punjabi meal, and at the center of langar too. In many gurdwaras the langar rotis are called prashada, the same word used for something received as a blessing. So the bread isn't just food. It's something given. Rolling rotis is seva with dough, and it uses all three of the sevas you met: the hands knead and roll, the mind teaches the new person how to turn the circle, and the flour itself may be bought with daswandh, the tenth that Sikhs give. It's a good place to learn, too. Grandmothers teach teenagers. Beginners make lopsided shapes, and nobody minds, because a lopsided roti tastes the same. In the biggest kitchens, like the Harmandir Sahib's, machines now help, but volunteers still roll by hand beside them. Think back to the bread in the stories. On day thirty-three, Guru Nanak chose the coarse bread of Bhai Lalo, a carpenter who earned it honestly, over the rich feast of a man who didn't. On day forty-six, Mata Khivi ran the kitchen at Khadur, and tradition remembers her langar for its care and its warmth. In these stories, bread carries the honesty of whoever earned it and the love of whoever made it. Roll a roti in langar and you join a long line: Lalo, Khivi, and every volunteer since. Round, warm, and shared.
screen: `ROTI, CALLED PRASHADA IN LANGAR.` · `ALL THREE SEVAS IN ONE BREAD.` · `LOPSIDED TASTES THE SAME.` · `LALO'S BREAD, KHIVI'S KITCHEN.` · then, large: `ROUND, WARM, SHARED.`

segments.voice: If you have bread nearby, a roti, a slice, a cracker, hold it in your hands; if not, picture one, warm from the pan. Think of all the hands behind it: whoever grew the wheat, milled the flour, mixed the dough, baked it, drove it, sold it. Then picture one person you could share it with, and see yourself tearing it in two and handing them the bigger half.
Rolling rotis. The seva of making langar's bread by hand, called prashada in many gurdwaras: something given, not just food.
Your line: round, warm, shared. The bigger half always goes to them. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 116 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A MEAL EVERYONE CAN EAT.`

117.title: A meal everyone can eat
117.hook: langar food is kept vegetarian so that anyone can share it
117.howItsDone: Gurdwaras serve a simple vegetarian langar, typically dal, a vegetable dish, rice and rotis, so that people of any faith or diet can eat it; Sikhs themselves hold differing views about eating meat at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rolling rotis: seva with dough, and bread called prashada. Your line was round, warm, shared.

Planning a party for a mixed group of friends is a puzzle. One doesn't eat pork. One eats only halal. One is vegetarian, one is vegan, one has a nut allergy, one just really hates mushrooms. You end up texting everyone, checking labels, making three versions of the same dish. Now multiply that by thousands of guests you've never met, from every religion and none, walking in off the street all day, every day, and nobody fills in a form. How do you feed them all without anyone having to ask what's in the pot? The langar's answer is simple, and it's an old one.
screen: `THE PARTY PUZZLE.` → `THOUSANDS OF GUESTS, NO FORMS.` → `NO ONE HAS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Langar is kept vegetarian. Dal, a pot of lentils. A vegetable dish. Rice, rotis, maybe yogurt, maybe kheer, a sweet rice pudding. Simple food, and nothing on the plate that would stop a guest from eating it. Think about who could walk in. Hindus who don't eat beef. Muslims and Jews who don't eat pork. Jains and some Hindus who eat no meat at all. Sikhs whose own practice keeps them vegetarian. Visitors with no religious rule who just want to be sure. With a vegetarian langar, none of them has to ask. The meal says welcome before anyone opens their mouth. That's the key idea: the food is shaped by the guests, not the cooks. The goal isn't a rule about what people should eat. It's making sure no one is left out of the row. Honestly, Sikhs themselves differ about meat in their own homes. Some are strictly vegetarian; others eat meat, and Sikh codes of conduct forbid meat that has been ritually slaughtered. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that fools argue over flesh and meat without understanding wisdom, and Sikhs read that passage in more than one way. But on the langar there's no argument: it's vegetarian, so everyone can eat. You don't have to be vegetarian to learn from this. The question works at any table: when I set out food, who could eat it, and who would be left out?

segments.voice: Picture a table in your home with five chairs, filled with people you know who eat differently: one who doesn't eat meat, one who avoids pork, one with an allergy, one who's picky, one who just needs something warm. Dal. The pot of lentils at the heart of langar, kept simple and vegetarian, so that no guest, of any faith or diet, has to ask what's in it.
Your line: everyone can eat this. No one has to ask what's in the pot. That's day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Cupped hands
118.hook: servers walk the rows and people receive with open, cupped hands
118.howItsDone: In langar, volunteers walk the rows serving the seated sangat, and in many gurdwaras people receive rotis, like karah prashad, in both hands cupped together, covering the plate with a hand when they have had enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dal: langar kept simple and vegetarian, so no guest has to ask. Your line was everyone can eat this.

Someone offers to pay for your coffee, and what do you say? No, no, I've got it. A friend offers to help you move: oh, don't worry about it. Someone gives you a compliment, and you wave it away before it lands. Giving can be easy while receiving feels awkward. Now sit down in the pangat. A volunteer comes down the row with a basket of warm rotis. When they reach you, you don't grab, and you don't wave them off. You lift both hands together, palms up, cupped like a bowl. And they place the bread right into them.
screen: `NO, NO, I'VE GOT IT.` → `GIVING IS EASY.` → `BOTH HANDS, PALMS UP.`

segments.voice: In langar, the servers walk the rows: one with a bucket of dal, one with a basket of rotis, one with a jug of water. You stay seated. They come to you. And in many gurdwaras you receive the roti the way you receive karah prashad, the sweet offering given at the end of worship: with both hands cupped together. The gesture says a lot without a word. It's open: nothing hidden, nothing held back. It's humble: you're below the giver's hands, waiting. And it's whole: you're not taking with one hand while the other holds your phone. There's a quiet lesson here for anyone who finds receiving hard. Seva teaches you to give without wanting thanks. Cupped hands teach you to receive without embarrassment. Both thin the ego. The one who can only give, and never receive, still keeps a little pride. The Japji has a bigger version. There Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that our actions bring us this body, but the door of liberation opens by God's grace, the nadar, the gracious glance. In that line, the greatest thing is received, not earned. So the cupped hands in the row are practice for something bigger. One more small courtesy. If you don't want more, you don't push the server away; you cover your plate with your hand, or lift a palm. If you do want more, you just hold your hands out again. Nobody keeps count.

segments.voice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, cupped together like a bowl, and notice how it feels to sit this way, open and empty; some find it peaceful, some strangely hard. Then think of something you were given recently and didn't quite receive, a kindness, a compliment, help you brushed off. Imagine it placed into your hands again, and this time, let it land.
Cupped hands. The way many receive roti and karah prashad in the gurdwara: both hands, open and together, fully there to receive.
Your line: receive fully. Open, humble, and whole, like a bowl. Day one hundred eighteen, done.

119.title: A small langar at home
119.hook: invite someone and feed them, with no agenda
119.howItsDone: Many Sikh families treat hospitality as an extension of langar, feeding guests and neighbors freely at home, alongside serving in the gurdwara kitchen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cupped hands: receiving fully, open and humble. Your line was receive fully.

Dinner invitations often come with something attached. We should really catch up. I want you to meet my brother. Let's talk about that project. Nothing wrong with that. But there's another kind: being fed for no reason at all. No favor to ask, no news to share. Someone just noticed you might be hungry, or tired, or alone, and put a plate in front of you. That kind of meal tends to be remembered, and it's the last langar lesson. For five days you've been inside the gurdwara's kitchen and its rows. Today it moves into yours.
screen: `DINNER WITH SOMETHING ATTACHED.` → `FED FOR NO REASON AT ALL.` → `FROM THEIR KITCHEN TO YOURS.`

segments.voice: Langar didn't begin as an institution. It began in a household. At Kartarpur, on day forty-one, Guru Nanak farmed his own fields and shared food with whoever came. Mata Khivi's kitchen at Khadur was a family kitchen with an open door. Today's huge langars grew out of homes that fed people. So a small langar at home isn't a copy of the real thing. It's closer to where the real thing started. What makes a meal a langar, even with only two people? This week has the answer. The pangat: nobody sits higher, so serve your guest the way you'd serve yourself, or better. The open door: the guest doesn't have to earn it or explain it. A meal everyone can eat: think about what they can eat before what you'd like to cook. Cupped hands: when they try to thank you too much, receive the thanks and let it go. Most of all, no agenda. You're not recruiting them, fixing them, or networking with them. You're feeding them. Remember the second pillar from day thirteen, vand chakna, sharing what you have? This is that pillar at your own table. It doesn't have to be fancy. Dal and rice. A sandwich for a coworker who skipped lunch. Soup for the neighbor home from the hospital. Look back and the week makes a path: kirtan filled the home, then the row, the open door, the bread, the simple meal, the cupped hands. Now the home fills up again, with a guest.
screen: `LANGAR BEGAN IN A HOUSEHOLD.` · `THE ROW, THE DOOR, THE PLATE.` · `NO AGENDA. JUST FEED THEM.` · `VAND CHAKNA AT YOUR TABLE.` · then, large: `A SMALL LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you could feed: someone who'd be surprised, who's been having a hard time, who's new around here, or who eats alone more than they'd like. Picture them at your table, on your step, or at their door with a container of food, what you'd make that they could eat and when you'd ask, and hold the picture until it feels possible. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers.

Vand chakna. Sharing what you have: today, feeding one person, freely, with no agenda. Your week: kirtan at home, pangat, the open door, rotis, a meal everyone can eat, cupped hands, and your own langar.
Your line: a small langar. Nothing attached, just a plate. Tomorrow, simran on the breath.
